title: ASU 2025-06 Modernizes the Accounting for Internal-Use Software and Website Development Costs
summary: Learn how FASB ASU 2025-06 changes internal-use software cost capitalization, website development guidance, transition, and implementation.
body_markdown:
In September 2025, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) issued Accounting Standards Update (ASU) 2025-06, *Intangibles—Goodwill and Other—Internal-Use Software (Subtopic 350-40): Targeted Improvements to the Accounting for Internal-Use Software* . The amendments modernize the accounting for internal-use software costs and respond to development practices that have evolved beyond the sequential project stages contemplated by existing guidance.


In practice, organizations will need to focus less on where a project sits within a prescribed development process. Instead, they will need documentation showing that the project is authorized, funded, and likely to be completed and used as intended.


ASU 2025-06 primarily changes when capitalization begins and what evidence supports that decision. The update retains many of the existing rules governing which costs qualify for capitalization. It removes the project-stage framework from ASC 350-40, incorporates relevant website-development guidance previously contained in ASC 350-50, and establishes a single principles-based recognition threshold in ASC 350-40.


## Why the Guidance Is Changing


Existing ASC 350-40 uses project stages (preliminary project, application development, and postimplementation-operation) to determine when internal-use software costs should be expensed or capitalized. ASC 350-50 applies a separate stage-based framework to website-development costs. Those models can be difficult to apply to agile and iterative projects in which planning, coding, testing, deployment, and refinement occur concurrently or repeatedly.


ASU 2025-06 eliminates reliance on prescribed development stages. Under the amended guidance, an entity begins capitalizing eligible costs when both of the following criteria are met:


1. Management has authorized and committed to funding the software project.
2. It is probable that the project will be completed and the software will be used to perform its intended function: the “probable-to-complete” recognition threshold.


These concepts are not entirely new. Existing ASC 350-40 already considers management authorization, committed funding, and probable completion. The amendment makes those criteria, rather than a project’s movement into a particular stage, the operative basis for determining when capitalization begins.


## Assessing Significant Development Uncertainty


In evaluating whether completion and intended use are probable, an entity must consider whether its software-development activities contain significant development uncertainty. The amendments identify two circumstances that require particular attention:


1. The software includes technological innovations or novel, unique, or unproven functions or features, and the related uncertainty has not been resolved through coding and testing.
2. The entity has not identified the software’s significant performance requirements or expects those requirements to continue to be substantially revised.


If significant development uncertainty exists, the probable-to-complete threshold may not be met until the uncertainty is resolved. Accordingly, entities will need concurrent evidence supporting both technological feasibility in the context of the project and the stability of significant performance requirements.


## What Changes for Website Development Costs


ASU 2025-06 supersedes ASC 350-50 as a separate accounting model and incorporates relevant website-development guidance into ASC 350-40. Website-development costs therefore become subject to the same amended recognition framework as other internal-use software costs.


This consolidation should not be interpreted to mean that all concepts previously applied to website development disappear. The accounting continues to depend on the nature of the activity and whether the related cost qualifies for capitalization. For example, qualifying software application and infrastructure development costs may be capitalized after the recognition threshold is met, while content input, data conversion, routine maintenance, and operating costs generally continue to be expensed as incurred. Costs of upgrades and enhancements may be capitalized when they provide additional functionality.


## What Does Not Change


Although the amendments change when capitalization begins, they generally do not change the underlying categories of eligible and ineligible costs. Qualifying direct development costs may be capitalized after the recognition criteria are met. Training, data conversion or migration, maintenance, and operating costs generally remain expensed as incurred.


Capitalization generally ceases when the software is substantially complete and ready for its intended use. The existing concepts governing amortization, impairment, and the evaluation of upgrades and enhancements also largely remain intact.


ASU 2025-06 does not amend the accounting for software to be sold, leased, or otherwise marketed under ASC 985-20. It also does not change the analysis used to determine whether software is within the scope of ASC 350-40 or ASC 985-20.


## Effective Date and Transition


The amendments are effective for all entities for annual reporting periods beginning after **December 15, 2027** , and for interim reporting periods within those annual reporting periods. Early adoption is permitted as of the beginning of an annual reporting period.


**An entity may adopt the amendments using one of three transition approaches:**


**Prospective transition.** Apply the amendments to new software costs incurred beginning in the period of adoption for all projects, including in-process projects.


**Modified transition.** Apply the amendments prospectively to new software costs for all projects. For an in-process project that does not meet the amended capitalization requirements but met the previous requirements, derecognize previously capitalized costs through a cumulative-effect adjustment to opening retained earnings or another appropriate component of equity or net assets.


**Retrospective transition.** Recast comparative periods and recognize a cumulative-effect adjustment as of the beginning of the earliest period presented.


The ASU also clarifies disclosure requirements for capitalized internal-use software costs. Entities should evaluate those requirements when updating their accounting policies and financial-reporting processes.


## Practical Implementation Considerations


Implementation will require more than a technical accounting policy update. Entities should consider whether their project-governance processes and internal controls produce sufficient evidence to support the capitalization date.


**Key actions include:**


- Updating accounting policies to replace project-stage references with the amended recognition criteria.
- Documenting management authorization and committed funding.
- Establishing how project teams will identify significant performance requirements and assess whether those requirements remain subject to substantial revision.
- Documenting how unresolved technological uncertainty is evaluated and when it is resolved through coding and testing.
- Coordinating among accounting, finance, information technology, engineering, and project-management personnel.
- Reviewing cost-tracking systems to distinguish qualifying development costs from training, data-conversion, maintenance, and operating costs.
- Evaluating the available transition methods and related disclosure requirements well in advance of adoption.


## The Bottom Line


Under existing guidance, the capitalization analysis focuses heavily on the project stage or the type of website-development activity. Under ASU 2025-06, the central question becomes whether authorized management has committed funding and whether completion and intended use are probable after considering unresolved technological uncertainty and the stability of significant performance requirements.


For many entities, the largest accounting effect will be the timing of capitalization and the evidence required to support that determination. The largest structural change is the consolidation of website-development guidance into ASC 350-40. Organizations that develop or implement internal-use software should begin evaluating their policies, documentation, systems, and controls now so they are prepared for adoption.

ASU 2025-06 updates the accounting guidance for internal-use software costs under ASC 350-40. It eliminates the project-stage framework and establishes a principles-based recognition threshold for determining when capitalization begins.


Eligible costs can begin to be capitalized when management has authorized and committed to funding the software project and it is probable that the project will be completed and used for its intended function.


The ASU supersedes ASC 350-50 as a separate accounting model and incorporates relevant website-development guidance into ASC 350-40. Website-development costs are therefore subject to the same amended recognition framework as other internal-use software costs.


Organizations should evaluate their accounting policies, project documentation, cost-tracking systems, and internal controls. They should also consider how they will document management authorization, committed funding, significant performance requirements, and unresolved technological uncertainty.
